notes.front: What are the canonical sections of an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) in the Nygard format?
notes.back:
Title · Status · Context · Decision · Consequences.
Status is one of proposed / accepted / deprecated / superseded. One to two pages, prose, no implementation detail.
notes.extra: Example: ADR-014: Use Cilium as the Container Network Interface (CNI) for all production clusters — Status: Accepted 2026-03-02.

notes.front: What belongs in the Context section of an ADR — and what does not?
notes.back: Forces, constraints, and facts that would be true regardless of which option wins. No opinions, no solution language. A reader should be able to reconstruct the world before the decision.
notes.extra: Example: ADR "Adopt Gateway API instead of Ingress NGINX": the Ingress API is frozen; 40 tenant namespaces carry 200+ vendor annotations; cross-namespace routing is needed; ownership of Transport Layer Security (TLS) termination is disputed between platform and app teams. Not: "Gateway API is clearly better."

notes.front: How do the Decision and Consequences sections of an ADR differ?
notes.back:
Decision: one imperative sentence, "We will …".
Consequences: every result, positive and negative, including new work created. If the consequences list has no downside, it is marketing, not an ADR.
notes.extra:
Example: Decision: "We will run one cluster per environment per region, not one cluster per team."
Consequences: stronger blast-radius isolation; higher per-cluster overhead; we now need a fleet manager (Cluster API + Argo CD ApplicationSets); tenant teams lose cluster-admin.

notes.front: Why record rejected alternatives in an ADR?
notes.back: It stops the decision being relitigated every time a new person joins or a vendor visits. The rejection reasons are often more valuable than the choice itself.
notes.extra: Example: "We considered Calico, Cilium and the cloud provider CNI. Rejected the cloud CNI because per-pod IP allocation exhausts our /24 subnets at ~200 pods per node." Six months later, "why not just use the default CNI?" has an answer in Git.

notes.front: When is an ADR status Superseded rather than Deprecated?
notes.back:
Superseded: a newer ADR replaces it — link both ways.
Deprecated: the decision is no longer relevant and nothing replaces it.
notes.extra:
Example: Superseded: "ADR-007 Helm-only deployments → superseded by ADR-031 Kustomize + Argo CD."
Deprecated: "ADR-009 Run Jenkins controllers on the cluster" after Continuous Integration (CI) moved out of platform scope entirely.

notes.front: Why are accepted ADRs treated as immutable?
notes.back: The record must show what was known and believed at the time. Editing history destroys the reason the document exists. Changes come from a new ADR that supersedes the old one.
notes.extra: Example: Rewriting "we chose etcd on local NVMe" into "we chose managed control planes" erases the 2026 reasoning about latency and cost that a 2028 reader needs to judge whether the constraints still hold.

notes.front: What is the sign an ADR is too long or in the wrong place?
notes.back: It contains implementation detail — Helm values, YAML, runbook steps. Those belong in the repo or runbook; the ADR links to them. Target: readable in five minutes.
notes.extra: Example: The Cilium ADR explains why eBPF datapath, Hubble observability and identity-based policy matter. It does not paste the CiliumNetworkPolicy schema or the values.yaml.

notes.front: What is the structure of a one-page memo?
notes.back:
1. Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF): the recommendation and its cost
  2. The decision you need from the reader, by when
  3. Three supporting points with evidence
  4. Risks, and what you are not proposing
  5. Next steps with owner and date
notes.extra: Example: BLUF: "Stop offering shared clusters to new tenants from Q2. Per-tenant clusters cut on-call pages by an estimated 40% (based on the 6 tenants already migrated) at +€9k/month."

notes.front: What does Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF) require, and what is a bad platform-team BLUF?
notes.back: First sentence = the recommendation, the cost, and ideally the number. The reader should be able to stop after one sentence and know what you want.
notes.extra:
Example: Bad: "This memo explores options for improving our cluster upgrade process."
Good: "Recommend automated weekly minor-version upgrades for all non-prod clusters, staffed at 0.5 FTE, starting March; this removes the 3-week prod lag we had on 1.31."

notes.front: What are the typical sections of an Amazon-style narrative (six-pager) and how is it read?
notes.back: Prose, no slides. Typical: Introduction & goal · Tenets · Current state · Lessons learned · Proposal & strategic priorities · FAQ · Appendices. The meeting opens with 20–30 minutes of silent reading, then discussion.
notes.extra: Example: A six-pager arguing for an Internal Developer Platform (IDP) layer on top of k8s. The FAQ pre-answers "Why not just give teams kubectl and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)?" so the meeting isn't spent there.

notes.front: What is the job of the FAQ section in an Amazon-style narrative?
notes.back: To state the hardest objections in the author's own words, sharper than the critics would, and answer them. It signals you have already stress-tested the proposal and moves the meeting past the obvious.
notes.extra: Example: "Q: Doesn't namespace multi-tenancy give us 90% of the isolation? A: Not for the payments workload: shared kernel, shared etcd, and API-server noisy-neighbour effects we measured at 1.2s p99 during a tenant's mass rollout."

notes.front: What are tenets in an Amazon narrative? Give one for a k8s platform.
notes.back: Non-negotiable principles, stated up front, used to resolve trade-offs later in the document and in the meeting. They are the tie-breakers.
notes.extra:
Example: "Paved road, not walled garden: tenants may leave the golden path, but they own on-call for what they build off it."
"No tenant-facing API ships without a deprecation policy."

notes.front: Rewrite: "Various options exist for secrets management and we think External Secrets Operator might be a reasonable direction."
notes.back:
"We will use External Secrets Operator (ESO) backed by HashiCorp Vault for all tenant secrets. Sealed Secrets and SOPS were rejected because both store ciphertext in Git and cannot rotate credentials."
Decision first, imperative voice, rejections with reasons.
notes.extra: Example: Test each sentence: could a reader act on it? "Might be a reasonable direction" gives them nothing to accept or reject.

notes.front: Why is structured writing called the most underrated marketability lever for architects?
notes.back: Writing is asynchronous proof of thinking. A memo or ADR travels to people you will never meet — executives, auditors, future hires — and it persists. Verbal influence evaporates after the meeting; a document can be cited in reviews, interviews and audits years later.
notes.extra: Example: The engineer who wrote the cluster-topology ADR is still "the person who thought about multi-cluster" two years on, even after the meetings are forgotten. It is also the artefact you show in a Solutions Architect interview.

notes.front: Which platform decisions deserve an ADR, and which don't?
notes.back: ADR when: hard to reverse, cross-team impact, or you'll be asked "why" in a year. Not for: reversible config, one-team choices, routine upgrades.
notes.extra:
Example: ADR: CNI choice, cluster topology, GitOps tool, secrets backend, Pod Security Standards level, ingress model.
No ADR: bumping the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) default target from 70% to 75%.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: "Explaining a hard thing simply is the visible proof of understanding." Why visible?
notes.back: Nobody can inspect your understanding directly. Simplification without loss is the only external signal that you hold the whole model, not just the vocabulary.
notes.extra: Example: "The scheduler is a loop: find pending pods, filter nodes that can't host them, score the rest, bind." One sentence that survives every follow-up question proves more than reciting all the scheduling plugins.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: What is the Feynman technique, applied to a platform topic?
notes.back:
1. Pick a concept
  2. Explain it in plain language to a non-expert
  3. Notice where you reach for jargon — that's the gap
  4. Go back to the source, then simplify again
notes.extra: Example: Explaining how a ClusterIP Service routes traffic. You say "kube-proxy programs iptables" — stop. Can you explain what that rule does to a packet? If not, that is where you read the code or docs.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: What is the ladder of abstraction, and how do you use it in a talk about GitOps?
notes.back: Move deliberately between concrete and abstract. Start concrete, rise to the principle, descend again to a different concrete case that the principle now explains.
notes.extra:
Example: Concrete: a developer changes replicas: 3 → 5 in a pull request; Argo CD syncs.
Abstract: desired state lives in Git; a controller reconciles continuously.
Concrete again: someone kubectl edits the Deployment — drift is detected and reverted. The principle predicts it.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: Structure for a ten-minute teaching talk.
notes.back: Hook (a pain the audience felt) → one core idea → three examples → a diagram or live demo → one thing they can do on Monday. Don't cover a topic; uncover one idea.
notes.extra: Example: Hook: "Your pods got evicted at 03:00 during the 1.30 upgrade." Core idea: node drains respect PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs), and nothing else. Monday action: add a PDB with maxUnavailable: 1 to every Deployment with more than one replica.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: What is the curse of knowledge? Platform example and fix.
notes.back: Once you know something you cannot imagine not knowing it, so you skip the steps the audience needs. Fix: start from the symptom the audience experiences, not the mechanism you know.
notes.extra: Example: Platform engineer to app team: "Just add a PodDisruptionBudget." The team doesn't know what a drain is. Start with: "Here is why your pods disappeared in pairs at 03:00."

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: Analogy vs model when teaching — how do you use both?
notes.back: Analogy gets the listener started, then breaks. Give the analogy, show exactly where it breaks, then give the real model. Never leave them with only the analogy.
notes.extra: Example: "Namespaces are like folders" → breaks: folders don't carry ResourceQuotas, RBAC scope or NetworkPolicy selectors → model: "a namespace is a scope for names plus a boundary for quota, access control and policy."

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: How do you explain to finance and executives why you want fewer, larger clusters?
notes.back: Translate into their currency: cost, risk, speed. Give the number, then the trade-off you are asking them to accept. No tool names.
notes.extra: Example: "Each cluster costs three control-plane nodes plus ~4 engineer-hours a month; 60 clusters is 240 hours. Consolidating to 12 frees ~1.5 FTE but concentrates blast radius, so we'd spend that capacity on tenant isolation." Not: "we'll use vCluster and hierarchical namespaces."

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: What is the one-sentence test before preparing a talk?
notes.back: If you cannot state the talk as one sentence a listener could repeat to a colleague, you don't have a talk yet — you have a topic.
notes.extra:
Example: Passes: "Tenants should never need to know what a node is; that is the whole job of the platform."
Fails: "An overview of our scheduling and autoscaling improvements."

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: How do you handle a hostile question during a talk, e.g. "Why didn't you just use Nomad?"
notes.back: Restate neutrally → answer the actual question in two sentences → concede the valid part → offer to continue afterwards. Never defend your ego, defend the reasoning.
notes.extra: Example: "Fair — orchestrator choice. We chose Kubernetes for the ecosystem: operators, policy engines, hiring pool. Nomad would have been simpler for our first ten services; it wouldn't be for the next two hundred. Happy to go deeper after."

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: Why prefer a hand-drawn request-path diagram over slides full of YAML?
notes.back: An audience can read or listen, not both. YAML on screen means they stop listening. Draw the path as you narrate so the drawing and the words arrive together; put the YAML in an appendix or repo link.
notes.extra: Example: Draw live: client → Gateway → HTTPRoute → Service → EndpointSlice → Pod, adding each hop as you explain it. The HTTPRoute manifest goes in the linked repo.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: Teaching pitfall: showing only the happy path. Why and example.
notes.back: People understand a system through its failure modes; the happy path teaches syntax, not the model.
notes.extra: Example: Teaching the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): show what happens when the metric is missing, when resources.requests are unset (utilisation can't be computed), and when it fights a Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) on the same Deployment.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: Why is an internal brown-bag session a cheap career lever?
notes.back: Repeatable visibility at near-zero cost: thirty minutes reaches forty engineers, leaves a recording and a document, and makes you the person people ask. Visibility compounds when the artefact is linkable.
notes.extra: Example: "How our cluster upgrade actually works" — record it, publish the doc, link it from the upgrade runbook. Every incident review that touches upgrades now points at your name.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::2 Public Speaking & Teaching
notes.front: How do you calibrate depth for a mixed audience (developers, security, management) in one talk?
notes.back: Layer it: first two minutes everyone understands, middle for the practitioners, last section explicitly flagged as "for those who run this." Signpost the transitions so people know when to tune in.
notes.extra: Example: Talk on image signing: (1) "we now refuse unsigned images in prod" — everyone; (2) how Sigstore/cosign signatures attach in CI — developers; (3) admission controller policy and key rotation — platform and security.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: What makes a decision meeting actually decide?
notes.back:
• Pre-read sent ≥48h ahead, with options written out
  • The decision phrased as a question with options
  • A named decider (not a vote)
  • Explicit criteria
  • A timebox
  • Decision, owner and date written down before anyone leaves
notes.extra: Example: "Decide: do tenant teams get cluster-admin on dev clusters? Options A/B/C in the doc. Decider: Head of Platform. 30 minutes. Criteria: blast radius, support load, developer velocity."

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: What are decision rights (decide / consult / input / inform) and why state them at the start?
notes.back: If you don't, everyone assumes they hold a veto. Naming the roles up front turns objections into input instead of blockers.
notes.extra: Example: Enforcing Pod Security Standards restricted by default: security is consulted, app tech leads give input, the platform lead decides, the CTO is informed. Say this in the first minute.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: How do you run a disagree and commit close?
notes.back: After the decider decides, ask each dissenter explicitly: "Can you commit to executing this even though you'd have chosen otherwise?" Record the answer. Commitment is to execution, not to agreement.
notes.extra: Example: Network team preferred Calico; decision is Cilium. Their commitment: own the migration runbook and the first two cluster cut-overs. Written in the decision record.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: Decision record vs meeting notes — what's the difference?
notes.back: Notes: what was said. Decision record: what was decided, by whom, why, which alternatives were rejected, and what would reopen it. The record feeds the ADR; the notes are disposable.
notes.extra: Example: "Reopen if Cilium enterprise pricing exceeds €X/node/year, or if we need Windows node pools." Without a reopen clause, every pricing rumour becomes a new argument.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: Anti-pattern: the status meeting disguised as a decision meeting. How do you fix it?
notes.back: If nobody has to choose between options with real trade-offs, cancel it or make it asynchronous. Convert every agenda item into a question with options, or drop it.
notes.extra: Example: "Review the upgrade plan" → "Decide: upgrade prod during business hours using canary clusters (A) or in a weekend window (B)." If the answer is obvious, it's an email, not a meeting.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: A stakeholder keeps blocking a platform change. How do you surface the real objection?
notes.back: Ask about consequences, not positions: "What would have to be true for this to work for you?" The real objection is usually operational or political, not the technical argument you've been having.
notes.extra: Example: App team refuses the new Gateway API ingress. Real reason after one question: they have no routing tests and a two-person on-call. Solution: platform writes the migration smoke test and moves them during their quiet week. The CNI debate was irrelevant.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: Stakeholder map for a k8s platform team: four groups and what each wants.
notes.back:
• Tenant developers: speed, fewer YAML foot-guns
  • App tech leads: predictability, control over their runtime
  • Security / compliance: evidence, enforced policy
  • Leadership / finance: cost, risk, headcount
The same decision needs four different one-liners.
notes.extra: Example: Enforcing image signing via admission control: devs — "one extra CI step, template provided"; tech leads — "no surprise blocks, dry-run for 30 days"; security — "audit log of every rejected image"; leadership — "closes finding 4 from the last audit at zero extra headcount."

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: What is a pre-mortem and how do you run one for a cluster migration?
notes.back: Before deciding, assume it is six months later and the project failed. Everyone silently writes why for five minutes; cluster the answers; the top three become mitigations or explicit decision criteria.
notes.extra: Example: Typical outputs: "stateful workloads on local persistent volumes couldn't move", "DNS cut-over broke external clients", "tenant teams weren't staffed for the change window." Each becomes a line in the plan with an owner.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: How do you stop the loudest engineer deciding by volume?
notes.back: Silent writing first (everyone writes their option and reasoning before any discussion), round-robin reading, decider speaks last. Put the options on the board so the argument is about artefacts, not people.
notes.extra: Example: Choosing a GitOps tool: five people write "Argo CD / Flux / neither, and why" on cards before anyone talks. The strongest argument for Flux came from the quietest person in the room.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: What does a well-done escalation look like?
notes.back: Both parties escalate together with a shared one-pager: agreed facts · the disagreement in one sentence · each option with the trade-off the other side cares about · the specific decision needed. The escalation target decides, not re-investigates.
notes.extra: Example: "Security wants NetworkPolicy default-deny on day one; platform wants a 90-day observe-only phase. Agreed: both end in default-deny. Decide the phase-in length."

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: What do you say in the last two minutes of every decision meeting?
notes.back: "We decided X. Owner is Y. It's recorded at Z. Anyone who can't commit?" Then send the record within the hour, before memories diverge.
notes.extra: Example: "We decided: Gateway API only for new services from 1 May. Owner: Saran. Record: ADR-036. Anyone who can't commit?" Silence is recorded as commitment.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: A stakeholder agreed in the meeting but undermines the decision afterwards. What do you do?
notes.back: Go direct and private. Refer to the recorded commitment. Ask what changed. If something material changed, reopen formally with a new ADR; if not, ask them to stop. Never tolerate silent drift — it teaches everyone that decisions are optional.
notes.extra: Example: After the "Gateway API only" decision a team keeps creating LoadBalancer Services. Conversation, not a policy: "You committed in ADR-036; what's blocking you?" Then, if needed, an admission policy with a dated exception.

notes.deck: Architect Skills (k8s platform)::3 Facilitation & Stakeholder Mgmt
notes.front: How do you handle a decision where the decider isn't in the room?
notes.back: Don't fake it. Produce the decision package instead: options, recommendation, dissent recorded, deadline for the decider. A recommendation with recorded dissent is a decision-ready artefact; a meeting that ends in "we'll check with X" is not.
notes.extra: Example: Head of Platform is out. The team produces: "Recommend option B (canary clusters). Network lead prefers A. Needs decision by Friday to hit the 1.31 window." Emailed as a one-pager.

notes.front: "What problem is this platform actually solving?" — bad vs good answer for a k8s platform.
notes.back: Bad: names the technology. Good: names the users, the pain, the measurable outcome. Kubernetes is the implementation; it is never the product.
notes.extra:
Example: Bad: "Providing Kubernetes to the organisation."
Good: "Cutting time from merged code to production for 30 product teams from days to under an hour, with security controls applied by default so teams don't need a per-deploy security review."

notes.front: What is a Job To Be Done (JTBD) for a platform user? Template and example.
notes.back: "When [situation], I want to [motivation], so that [outcome]." It describes the user's goal, never a platform feature. The JTBD tells you which roadmap item matters.
notes.extra: Example: "When I have a new service, I want it running in staging with logs, metrics and a URL, so I can demo it on Thursday." Not: "I want a namespace." This is why the onboarding template matters more than the CNI.

notes.front: Cheap user-research methods for a platform team.
notes.back:
• Contextual inquiry: watch a developer onboard a service, without helping
  • Five to eight 30-minute interviews: "walk me through the last time you deployed"
  • Mine support tickets and the Slack help channel
  • Measure time-to-first-deploy
Five interviews surface most of the problems.
notes.extra: Example: Watching one developer onboard revealed that the four-ticket process (namespace, RBAC, secrets, DNS) had a fifth hidden step: asking in Slack which Helm chart version to use. No ticket recorded it.

notes.front: Platform as a product vs platform as a mandate — how do you tell which one you have?
notes.back:
Product: teams adopt because it's better; adoption is a tracked metric; the roadmap is driven by user need. Mandate: teams use it because they must; the platform optimises for its own operability.
Signal: do teams ask you for features, or route around you?
notes.extra: Example: A team quietly running its own Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) cluster is the loudest possible user-research finding.

notes.front: Roadmap trade-off: multi-cluster service mesh vs self-service namespace onboarding. How do you decide?
notes.back: Against the problem statement and evidence, not against which is more interesting. Write down what you are not doing and the condition under which you'd revisit.
notes.extra: Example: 20 teams wait three days for a namespace; two teams need cross-cluster mutual TLS. Onboarding wins. Recorded: "Mesh deferred to Q4; revisit if a third team needs cross-cluster mTLS or if the payments workload's compliance deadline moves."

notes.front: What is a golden path (paved road) and what is the product decision behind it?
notes.back: An opinionated, fully supported default: template repo, Helm chart or Backstage template, CI pipeline, observability wired in. The decision: which 80% of use cases you make excellent, and that the other 20% get "you can, but you own it."
notes.extra: Example: Golden path = stateless HTTP service, Deployment + HTTPRoute + ServiceMonitor + PDB, one values.yaml. Off-path (StatefulSets with local storage, Windows) is allowed and unsupported.

notes.front: Which metrics measure the platform as a product, as opposed to cluster operations?
notes.back: Time-to-first-deploy for a new service · deploy frequency and lead time (DORA metrics) · % of workloads on the golden path · tickets per deploy · developer satisfaction · share of the platform team's time on unplanned work.
notes.extra: Example: Node CPU utilisation and etcd latency are operations metrics — necessary, but they say nothing about whether tenants are better off. Report both, but lead with the product ones.

notes.front: How do you say no to a feature request product-style? Example: a team wants Windows nodes.
notes.back: Understand the underlying job → quantify demand → name the full cost → offer an alternative → record it so the next request starts from evidence.
notes.extra: Example: Job: one legacy .NET Framework service. Demand: one team. Cost: separate node pool, separate image pipeline, half the ecosystem (CNI features, policy engines) unsupported. Alternative: port to .NET 8 on Linux, or run it outside the platform with a documented exception.

notes.front: What is the internal customer trap?
notes.back: Treating tenants as captive, so value is never validated and the platform team gets no honest feedback. Counter it by acting as if they could leave.
notes.extra: Example: Publish a Service Level Objective (SLO), a roadmap and a deprecation policy; hold weekly office hours; show teams what it costs to run outside the platform. If they still stay, that's evidence.

notes.front: What does a good deprecation look like on a platform?
notes.back: Announce with a date (at least two release cycles out) · provide a migration path and tooling · show each tenant exactly what of theirs is affected · warn in-cluster · then enforce. Silence until enforcement is the failure mode.
notes.extra: Example: Removing Ingress NGINX annotations in favour of Gateway API HTTPRoute: dashboard from admission-webhook telemetry listing affected Ingresses per namespace, a conversion script, kubectl apply warnings for 60 days, then rejection.

notes.front: How do you make the opportunity cost of platform hygiene visible on the roadmap?
notes.back: Every quarter spent on upgrades and CVE patching is a quarter not spent on what tenants asked for. Reserve a fixed capacity for hygiene and put the rest on the roadmap so the split is a decision, not a default.
notes.extra: Example: "30% of capacity is reserved for upgrades, patching and toil reduction; the remaining 70% is on the public roadmap. When 1.31 slipped, that came out of the 30%, not out of self-service onboarding."

notes.front: How do you write a problem statement before proposing a solution?
notes.back: Who · what pain · evidence · what it costs · what "solved" looks like. Only after that name a tool.
notes.extra: Example: "New services take four days to reach staging (measured across 11 onboardings in Q1) because namespace, RBAC, secrets and DNS are four separate tickets. Solved means under one hour, self-service, zero tickets." Only now discuss Crossplane or a Backstage template.

notes.front: What is the difference between a feature request and a problem report, and why does it matter for the roadmap?
notes.back: A feature request is the user's proposed solution; a problem report is the pain. Log the pain, not the solution, or the roadmap becomes a list of other people's designs.
notes.extra: Example: Request: "Give us cluster-admin on dev." Problem: "We can't install CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs) for the operator we're evaluating." Solution that fits: a self-service, namespaced operator catalogue — not cluster-admin.

notes.front: How do the four skills combine in one platform initiative?
notes.back: Product thinking finds the problem worth solving → structured writing turns it into a memo or ADR → facilitation gets the decision made and committed to → speaking and teaching drive adoption. Skipping any one is where platform initiatives usually die.
notes.extra: Example: Self-service onboarding: interviews showed the 4-day wait (product) → one-page memo with BLUF and cost (writing) → decision meeting with named decider, network team commits (facilitation) → brown-bag and template walkthrough for tenants (teaching).
